title: Dat Erdmänneken
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 91. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly. This tale is in Low German (Plattdeutsch); the glossary gives the High German equivalent for each dialect form.
about: Be warned at the first line: KHM 91 is printed from beginning to end in Low German (Plattdeutsch), the old speech of the north rather than the High German of most of the collection, so Et was mal en rik Künig west is not broken German but dialect for Es war einmal ein reicher König. Three king’s daughters eat the one forbidden apple and sink a hundred fathoms under the earth; three huntsmen take up quarters in a castle in the wood, and only the youngest — the one the others call stupid Hans — thrashes the little man who has been stealing their bread, and so learns from the Erdmänneken (the earth-man, or gnome, of the title) where the daughters are kept, each with a many-headed dragon in her lap to delouse. He goes down the well alone, is cut loose there by his own companions, and comes up again by a flute that calls the earth-men out of the ground. Grimm glosses the hardest dialect words in round brackets inside the 1857 text — Telgen (Zweige), Teite (Vater), Owen (Ofen) — and those parentheses are his, not ours.

sentences.t: Et was mal en rik Künig west, de hadde drei Döchter had, de wören alle Dage in den Schlottgoren spazeren gaen,
sentences.l: There was once a rich king been, he had three daughters had, they were every day in the castle-garden gone walking,
sentences.i: There was once a rich king who had three daughters, and every day they went walking in the castle garden,
sentences.n: The whole tale is told in Low German (Plattdeutsch), the speech of the north — not the High German of most of the collection — so nearly every word looks a little foreign. Here: Et = ‘es’, was = ‘war’ (not the High German ‘was’, what), mal = ‘einmal’, en = ‘ein’, rik = ‘reich’, west = ‘gewesen’, de = ‘der/die’, hadde = ‘hatte’, had = ‘gehabt’, wören = ‘waren’, gaen = ‘gegangen’. Low German doubles the perfect: “de hadde drei Döchter had” is literally ‘who had three daughters had’, and “wören ... gaen” ‘were ... gone’. English can keep only one half, so the literal keeps one.

sentences.t: un de Künig, dat was so en Leivhawer von allerhand wackeren Bömen west:
sentences.l: and the king, he was such a lover of all manner of fine trees been:
sentences.i: and the king was such a lover of all manner of fine trees:
sentences.n: Leivhawer = ‘Liebhaber’, a lover or fancier of a thing; wackeren = ‘wackeren’, fine, sturdy, splendid; Bömen = ‘Bäumen’. The loose syntax — the subject named first, then picked up again by dat, ‘that’ — is the spoken storyteller’s voice, and it runs through the whole tale.

sentences.t: un einen, den hadde he so leiv had, dat he denjenigen, de ümme en Appel dervon plückede, hunnerd Klafter unner de Eere verwünschede.
sentences.l: and one [tree], that one he had so dear had, that he the one who plucked but an apple from it, a hundred fathoms under the earth spell-cursed.
sentences.i: and one tree he held so dear that he laid a spell on anyone who picked so much as an apple from it, sending them a hundred fathoms under the earth.
sentences.n: [tree] is supplied by us: the German has only einen, ‘one’, with the noun carried over from Bömen in the clause before. leiv had = ‘lieb gehabt’, held dear; ümme = ‘um’, here ‘for the sake of’; dervon = ‘davon’; verwünschede = ‘verwünschte’, wished away by a spell — the curse that sets the whole tale going. A Klafter is a fathom, an old measure of depth of about six feet.

sentences.t: Als et nu Hervest war, da worden de Appel an den einen Baume so raut ase Blaud.
sentences.l: When it now autumn was, then became the apples on the one tree so red as blood.
sentences.i: When autumn came, the apples on that one tree turned as red as blood.
sentences.n: Hervest = ‘Herbst’; worden = ‘wurden’, became (not the participle ‘geworden’); raut = ‘roth/rot’; ase = ‘als/wie’; Blaud = ‘Blut’. de Appel is plural here — Low German keeps the same form for one apple and many.

sentences.t: De drei Döchter gungen alle Dage unner den Baum un seihen to ov nig de Wind ’n Appel herunner schlagen hädde, awerst se fannen ir Levedage kienen,
sentences.l: The three daughters went every day under the tree and looked to see whether not the wind an apple down had struck, but they found their life-days none,
sentences.i: The three daughters went under the tree every day and looked to see whether the wind had not knocked an apple down, but never in all their days did they find one,
sentences.n: gungen = ‘gingen’; seihen to = ‘sahen zu’, looked to see; ov = ‘ob’; nig = ‘nicht’; ’n = ‘einen’, the article — not the pronoun ‘ihn’ that ’n is elsewhere; herunner schlagen = ‘herunterschlagen’, to strike down, a separable verb with its particle standing out in front of it; fannen = ‘fanden’; “ir Levedage” = ‘ihr Lebtage’, an old accusative of time, in all their days; kienen = ‘keinen’.

sentences.t: un de Baum de satt so vull, dat he breken wull, un de Telgen (Zweige) hungen bis up de Eere.
sentences.l: and the tree, it sat so full that it break wanted, and the boughs (twigs) hung down to the earth.
sentences.i: and the tree hung so full that it was near breaking, and the branches hung down to the ground.
sentences.n: “satt so vull” = ‘saß so voll’, was so laden; wull = ‘wollte’ — with another verb, ‘wollen’ often means ‘was on the point of’ rather than ‘wished’; he = ‘er’, the tree, which is masculine. (Zweige) is the Grimms’ own gloss, printed in the 1857 text: Telgen is the northern word for boughs, so they supplied the High German. Every round-bracketed word in this tale is theirs, not ours.

sentences.t: Da gelustede den jungesten Künigskinne gewaldig
sentences.l: Then lusted the youngest king’s-child mightily
sentences.i: Then the youngest king’s child was seized with a mighty longing
sentences.n: An impersonal construction: ‘es gelüstete den ... gewaltig’ — the longing is the subject and the person stands in the dative (Künigskinne = ‘Königskinde’, an old dative in ‑e). gelustede = ‘gelüstete’; gewaldig = ‘gewaltig’, here adverbial. The child is grammatically neuter, Kind, and so is called et, ‘it’, all through — though she is one of the daughters.

sentences.t: un et segde to sinen Süstern „use Teite (Vater), de hett us viel to leiv, ase dat he us verwünschen deihe: ik glöve dat he dat nur wegen de frümden Lude dahen hat.“
sentences.l: and it said to its sisters, “our Teite (father), he has us far too dear, than that he us bewitch would: I believe that he that only on account of the strange folk done has.”
sentences.i: and she said to her sisters, “Our father holds us far too dear to lay his curse on us; I think he only said it on account of outsiders.”
sentences.n: Teite is a northern nursery word for father, and (Vater) is the Grimms’ own gloss. use = ‘unser’; hett = ‘hat’; us = ‘uns’; “to leiv” = ‘zu lieb’; “ase dat” = ‘als daß’, the frame ‘too ... to ...’; deihe = ‘täte’, a subjunctive, would do; glöve = ‘glaube’; “frümden Lude” = ‘fremden Leute’, strangers, outsiders; dahen = ‘gethan’.

sentences.t: Un indes plücked dat Kind en gans dicken Appel af un sprunk fur sinen Süstern
sentences.l: And meanwhile plucked the child a quite fat apple off and sprang before its sisters
sentences.i: And with that the child picked off a good fat apple and sprang out in front of her sisters
sentences.n: indes = ‘indes’, meanwhile, with that; “plücked ... af” = ‘pflückte ab’, another separable verb with its particle thrown to the end; gans = ‘ganz’, quite — not the High German ‘Gans’, goose, which it is spelled like; dicken = fat, plump; sprunk = ‘sprang’; fur = ‘vor’.

sentences.t: un segde „a, nu schmecket mal, mine lewen Süsterkes, nu hew ik doch min Levedage so wat schones no nig schmecket.“
sentences.l: and said, “ah, now taste once, my dear little-sisters, now have I surely my life-days such a fine thing not yet tasted.”
sentences.i: and said, “Ah, taste this, my dear sisters — never in all my days have I tasted anything so fine.”
sentences.n: lewen = ‘lieben’; Süsterkes = ‘Schwesterchen’, the northern diminutive plural; hew = ‘habe’; “min Levedage” = ‘mein Lebtage’, in all my life; “so wat schones” = ‘so was Schönes’; “no nig” = ‘noch nicht’; schmecket here = ‘geschmeckt’, tasted.

sentences.t: Da beeten de beiden annern Künigsdöchter auch mal in den Appel,
sentences.l: Then bit the two other king’s-daughters also once into the apple,
sentences.i: Then the two other king’s daughters bit into the apple as well,
sentences.n: beeten = ‘bissen’, the past plural of ‘beißen’ — not the Low German beeten meaning ‘a little’, which is a different word of the same spelling. auch is here in its High German form; the tale writes auck a few lines further on, and both stand.

sentences.t: un da versünken se alle drei deip unner de Eere, dat kien Haan mer danach krähete.
sentences.l: and then sank they all three deep under the earth, that no cock more after it crowed.
sentences.i: and then all three sank deep under the earth, so deep that no cock crowed after them again.
sentences.n: versünken = ‘versanken’; deip = ‘tief’; kien = ‘kein’; Haan = ‘Hahn’; mer = ‘mehr’; krähete = ‘krähte’. “Es kräht kein Hahn danach” is a set phrase — not a soul asks after it; they are gone without trace.

sentences.t: As et da Middag is, da wull se de Künig do Diske roopen, do sind se nirgends to finnen:
sentences.l: As it then midday is, then wanted the king them to table call, then are they nowhere to find:
sentences.i: When midday came and the king would call them to table, they were nowhere to be found:
sentences.n: The tale slips into the present tense here and keeps sliding between present and past to the end — the storyteller’s voice, not a slip of the pen; the literal follows it, the idiomatic evens it out. As = ‘als’; wull = ‘wollte’; “do Diske” = ‘zu Tische’; roopen = ‘rufen’; “sind ... to finnen” = ‘sind zu finden’.

sentences.t: he söket se so viel im Schlott un in Goren, awerst he kun se nig finnen.
sentences.l: he seeks them so much in the castle and in garden, but he could them not find.
sentences.i: he searched and searched for them in the castle and in the garden, but he could not find them.
sentences.n: söket = ‘sucht’; “so viel” is this tale’s favourite intensifier — ever so much — and it is used alike of searching, screaming, hugging and begging; Schlott = ‘Schloß’; Goren = ‘Garten’; awerst = ‘aber’; kun = ‘konnte’.

sentences.t: Da werd he so bedröwet un let dat ganse Land upbeien (aufbieten),
sentences.l: Then becomes he so grieved and let the whole land be summoned (called out),
sentences.i: Then he grew so grieved that he had the whole country called out to search,
sentences.n: werd = ‘wird’; bedröwet = ‘betrübt’; ganse = ‘ganze’. upbeien carries the Grimms’ own gloss (aufbieten) — to summon, to call out the country, as a ruler calls out his people.

sentences.t: un wer ünne sine Döchter wier brechte, de sull ene davon tor Fruen hewen.
sentences.l: and whoever him his daughters back brought, he should one of them to wife have.
sentences.i: and whoever brought him his daughters back should have one of them to wife.
sentences.n: ünne = ‘ihm’ — and also ‘ihn’; Low German has the one form for both, and it recurs on nearly every line from here on. sine = ‘seine’; wier = ‘wieder’; brechte = ‘brächte’, subjunctive; sull = ‘sollte’; ene = ‘eine’; “tor Fruen” = ‘zur Frau’; hewen = ‘haben’, to have — not the Low German word for heaven that hewen is in other tales.

sentences.t: Da gahet so viele junge Lude uwer Feld un söket, dat is gans ut der Wiese (über alle Maßen),
sentences.l: Then go so many young folk over field and seek, that is quite out of the ordinary (beyond all measure),
sentences.i: Then so many young men went out over the fields to search that it passed all bounds,
sentences.n: gahet = ‘gehen’; Lude = ‘Leute’; uwer = ‘über’. “ut der Wiese” is ‘aus der Weise’, out of the usual way — and (über alle Maßen) is the Grimms’ own gloss on it. Despite the spelling the word is not ‘Wiese’, meadow.

sentences.t: denn jeder hadde de drei Kinner geren had, wiil se wören gegen jedermann so fründlig un so schön von Angesichte west.
sentences.l: for everyone had the three children gladly had, because they were toward everyone so friendly and so fair of face been.
sentences.i: for everyone had been fond of the three children, because they had been so kind to all and so fair of face.
sentences.n: “geren had” = ‘gern gehabt’, been fond of; Kinner = ‘Kinder’; wiil = ‘weil’; fründlig = ‘freundlich’; Angesichte = ‘Angesicht’, countenance. The doubled perfect wören ... west (‘waren ... gewesen’) is the same northern habit as in the tale’s opening line.

sentences.t: Un et togen auck drei Jägerburschen ut,
sentences.l: And there set also three huntsmen’s-lads out,
sentences.i: And three young huntsmen also set out,
sentences.n: et = ‘es’, the empty placeholder subject of ‘es zogen drei aus’; “togen ... ut” = ‘zogen aus’, set out; auck = ‘auch’. A Jägerbursche is a huntsman’s lad, servant to a huntsman.

sentences.t: un ase da wol en acht Dage rieset hadden, da kummet se up en grot Schlot, da woren so hübsche Stoben inne west,
sentences.l: and when they there a good eight days travelled had, then come they upon a great castle, there were such fine rooms inside been,
sentences.i: and when they had been travelling some eight days, they came upon a great castle, and there were fine chambers within,
sentences.n: “wol en acht Dage” = ‘wohl an die acht Tage’, a good eight days; rieset = ‘gereist’; grot = ‘groß’; Schlot = ‘Schloß’ — spelled Schlott a line later; spelling in this text is nowhere fixed. Stoben = ‘Stuben’, rooms; inne = ‘drinnen’.

sentences.t: un in einen Zimmer is en Disch decket, darup wören so söte Spisen, de sied noch so warme dat se dampet,
sentences.l: and in one room is a table laid, thereupon were such sweet dishes, they are still so warm that they steam,
sentences.i: and in one room a table stood laid, with such delicious dishes on it, still so warm that they were steaming,
sentences.n: decket = ‘gedeckt’; darup = ‘darauf’; söte = ‘süße’, here in the older sense of savoury, delicious, not sugared; Spisen = ‘Speisen’; sied = ‘sind’ — not the Low German ‘seit’, since, that it is spelled like; dampet = ‘dampfen’.

sentences.t: awerst in den ganzen Schlott is kien Minsk to hören noch to seihen.
sentences.l: but in the whole castle is no person to hear nor to see.
sentences.i: but in the whole castle there was not a soul to be heard or seen.
sentences.n: Minsk = ‘Mensch’; “to hören noch to seihen” = ‘zu hören noch zu sehen’; seihen = ‘sehen’.

sentences.t: Do wartet se noch en halwen Dag,
sentences.l: Then wait they still a half day,
sentences.i: Then they waited another half day,
sentences.n: Do = ‘da/dann’; halwen = ‘halben’. Low German makes the plural of a verb in ‑et where High German has ‑en, so wartet is ‘warten’, they wait.

sentences.t: un de Spiesen bliewet immer warme un dampet, bis up et lest,
sentences.l: and the dishes stay ever warm and steam, until at the last,
sentences.i: and the dishes stayed warm and steaming all the while, until at last,
sentences.n: Spiesen is the same word as Spisen a moment ago, spelled otherwise; bliewet = ‘bleiben’; “bis up et lest” = ‘bis aufs letzte’, at long last.

sentences.t: da weret se so hungerig, dat se sik derbie settet un ettet,
sentences.l: then become they so hungry that they themselves down to it set and eat,
sentences.i: they grew so hungry that they sat down to it and ate,
sentences.n: weret = ‘werden’; hungerig is the older form of ‘hungrig’; derbie = ‘dabei’; settet = ‘setzen’; ettet = ‘essen’.

sentences.t: un macket mit en anner ut, se wüllen up den Schlotte wuhnen bliewen,
sentences.l: and make with one another out, they would in the castle dwelling stay,
sentences.i: and settled it between them that they would stay and live in the castle,
sentences.n: “macket ... ut” = ‘machen aus’, agree, settle between themselves — a separable verb with its particle at the end; “mit en anner” = ‘miteinander’; wüllen = ‘wollen’; “wuhnen bliewen” = ‘wohnen bleiben’, stay living.

sentences.t: un wüllen darümme loosen, dat eine in Huse blev un de beiden annern de Dochter söketen;
sentences.l: and would therefore draw lots, that one at home stayed and the two others the daughters sought;
sentences.i: and would draw lots for it, so that one stayed at home while the other two went looking for the daughters;
sentences.n: darümme = ‘darum’; loosen = ‘losen’, to draw lots; Huse = ‘Hause’; blev = ‘bliebe’; söketen = ‘suchten’. “de Dochter” is plural here though it has the shape of a singular.

sentences.t: dat doet se auck, un dat Loos dreppet den ölesten.
sentences.l: that do they also, and the lot falls to the eldest.
sentences.i: and so they did, and the lot fell to the eldest.
sentences.n: doet = ‘tun’; Loos = ‘Los’, the lot, in the 1857 spelling; dreppet = ‘trifft’, here in the sense ‘falls to’; ölesten = ‘ältesten’.

sentences.t: Den annern Dag da gaet de twei jüngesten söken, un de öleste mot to Huse bliewen.
sentences.l: The next day then go the two youngest to seek, and the eldest must at home stay.
sentences.i: The next day the two younger ones went off to search, and the eldest had to stay at home.
sentences.n: “Den annern Dag” is an accusative of time, ‘the next day’ — German marks a stretch of time by case alone, with no preposition. twei = ‘zwei’; jüngesten = ‘jüngsten’; mot = ‘muß’.

sentences.t: Am Middage kümmt der so en klein klein Männeken un hölt um ’n Stükesken Braud ane,
sentences.l: At midday comes there such a little little manikin and asks for a little-piece of bread,
sentences.i: At midday a tiny little man came and begged for a little piece of bread,
sentences.n: der here = ‘da’, there; the doubled “klein klein” is the storyteller’s way of saying very small indeed; Männeken = ‘Männchen’, manikin — the earth-man of the title; “hölt ... ane” = ‘hält an um’, asks for, petitions for, with the particle split off to the end; Stükesken = ‘Stückchen’; Braud = ‘Brot’.

sentences.t: da nümmt he von dem Braude, wat he da funnen hädde, un schnitt en Stücke rund umme den Braud weg un will ünne dat giewen,
sentences.l: then takes he of the bread that he there found had, and cuts a piece round about the loaf away and will him that give,
sentences.i: so he took some of the bread he had found there, and cut a piece right round the loaf, and was going to give it to him,
sentences.n: nümmt = ‘nimmt’; wat = ‘was’, here doing the work of a relative pronoun, ‘which’; funnen = ‘gefunden’; “schnitt ... weg” = ‘schnitt weg’; umme = ‘um’; giewen = ‘geben’. Cutting round the loaf is how a round country loaf is cut — a ring taken off the outside, not a slice.

sentences.t: indes dat he et ünne reiket, lett et dat kleine Männeken fallen
sentences.l: while that he it him hands, lets it the little manikin fall
sentences.i: but just as he handed it to him, the little man let it fall
sentences.n: “indes dat” = ‘indem/während’, just as; reiket = ‘reicht’; “lett ... fallen” = ‘läßt fallen’, drops. Mind the pronouns: et is the bread, ünne the little man, and dat kleine Männeken is the subject of the second half — it stands after the verb because the indes-clause has taken the first slot.

sentences.t: un segd he sulle dok so gut sin un giewen ün dat Stücke wier.
sentences.l: and says he should so good be and give him the piece back.
sentences.i: and said would he be so good as to give him the piece again.
sentences.n: segd = ‘sagt’; sulle = ‘sollte’; dok = ‘doch’, a coaxing particle with no single English word; sin = ‘sein’, to be — the same spelling that means ‘his’ elsewhere in this tale; ün = ‘ihm’; wier = ‘wieder’. “so gut sein und ...” is the ordinary polite formula, be so good as to.

sentences.t: Da will he dat auck doen un bucket sik,
sentences.l: Then will he that also do and bends himself down,
sentences.i: He was ready enough to do it and bent down,
sentences.n: doen = ‘thun/tun’; “bucket sik” = ‘bückt sich’, stoops.

sentences.t: mit des nümmt dat Männeken en Stock un päckt ünne bie den Haaren un giwt ünne düete Schläge.
sentences.l: with that takes the manikin a stick and seizes him by the hair and gives him sound blows.
sentences.i: and with that the little man took a stick, seized him by the hair, and gave him a sound beating.
sentences.n: “mit des” = ‘mit dem/damit’, with that; päckt = ‘packt’; bie = ‘bei’; düete = ‘tüchtige’, sound, hearty — the same word turns up below as duet.

sentences.t: Den anneren Dag, da is de tweide to Hus bliewen, den geit et nicks better.
sentences.l: The next day, then is the second at home stayed, to him goes it nothing better.
sentences.i: The next day the second stayed at home, and it went no better with him.
sentences.n: anneren = ‘anderen’; tweide = ‘zweite’; Hus = ‘Haus’; den = ‘dem’, a dative — ‘es geht ihm’, it goes for him, is the impersonal way German reports how a person fares; nicks = ‘nichts’; better = ‘besser’.

sentences.t: Ase de beiden annern da den Avend nah Hus kümmet, da segd de öleste „no, wie hätt et die dann gaen?“
sentences.l: When the two others there in the evening home come, then says the eldest, “well, how has it gone for you then?”
sentences.i: When the other two came home that evening, the eldest said, “Well, how did it go with you?”
sentences.n: nah = ‘nach’, to — not ‘nah’, near, which it is spelled like; kümmet = ‘kommen’; no = ‘nun/na’, the little opening ‘well’; hätt = ‘hat’ here, not ‘hätte’; die = ‘dir’, to you — in this tale die is very often the pronoun and not the article; gaen = ‘gegangen’.

sentences.t: „O, et geit mie gans schlechte.“
sentences.l: “Oh, it goes with me quite badly.”
sentences.i: “Oh, it went badly enough with me.”
sentences.n: geit = ‘geht’; mie = ‘mir’; gans = ‘ganz’; schlechte = ‘schlecht’ with the old adverbial ‑e.

sentences.t: Da klaget se sik enanner ere Naud,
sentences.l: Then lament they to one another their distress,
sentences.i: So they complained to one another of their trouble,
sentences.n: klaget = ‘klagen’; “sik enanner” = ‘sich einander’; ere = ‘ihre’; Naud = ‘Noth’, distress, hard usage.

sentences.t: awerst den jungesten hadden se nicks davonne sagd,
sentences.l: but to the youngest had they nothing of it said,
sentences.i: but they had said nothing of it to the youngest,
sentences.n: jungesten = ‘jüngsten’; davonne = ‘davon’; sagd = ‘gesagt’.

sentences.t: den hadden se gar nig lien (leiden) mogt un hadden ünne jummer den dummen Hans heiten, weil he nig recht van de Weld was.
sentences.l: him had they not at all suffer (endure) liked and had him always the stupid Hans called, because he not right of the world was.
sentences.i: they could not stand him at all, and had always called him stupid Hans, because he was not quite of this world.
sentences.n: lien carries the Grimms’ own gloss (leiden): “nicht leiden mögen” is to be unable to bear someone. mogt = ‘gemocht’; jummer = ‘immer’; heiten = ‘geheißen’, called; van = ‘von’; Weld = ‘Welt’; was = ‘war’. “nicht recht von der Welt” says he was simple, not sharp in worldly things — the youngest brother of a hundred tales.

sentences.t: Den dritten Dag, da blivt de jungeste to Hus, da kümmet dat kleine Männeken wier un hölt um en Stücksken Braud an;
sentences.l: The third day, then stays the youngest at home, then comes the little manikin again and asks for a little piece of bread;
sentences.i: On the third day the youngest stayed at home, and the little man came again and begged for a little piece of bread;
sentences.n: blivt = ‘bleibt’; Stücksken = ‘Stückchen’, the same word spelled Stükesken above. Here the separable particle stands at the end as an, where earlier it was ane — the tale is indifferent to such endings.

sentences.t: da he ünne dat giewen hätt, let he et wier fallen
sentences.l: when he it to him given has, lets he it again fall
sentences.i: and when he had given it to him, he let it fall again
sentences.n: hätt = ‘hat’; let = ‘läßt’. The subject changes inside the sentence: the he who gives is the young huntsman, the he who drops it is the little man.

sentences.t: un segd he mügte dock so gut sien un reicken ünne dat Stücksken wier.
sentences.l: and says he might so good be and hand him the little piece again.
sentences.i: and said would he be so good as to hand him the piece once more.
sentences.n: mügte = ‘möchte’; dock = ‘doch’; sien = ‘sein’; reicken = ‘reichen’. This is a request reported in the subjunctive — German reports speech by the mood of the verb rather than by a word for ‘that’, and this tale does it constantly.

sentences.t: Da segd he to den kleinen Männeken „wat! kannst du dat Stücke nig sulwens wier up nümmen,
sentences.l: Then says he to the little manikin, “what! can you the piece not yourself again up take,
sentences.i: Then he said to the little man, “What! Can you not pick the piece up again yourself,
sentences.n: sulwens = ‘selbst’; “up nümmen” = ‘aufnehmen’, pick up, with the particle standing free. du is simply ‘you’, the familiar singular — used here to a small stranger.

sentences.t: wenn du die de Möhe nig mal um dine dägliche Narunge giewen wust, so bist du auck nich werth, dat du et etest.“
sentences.l: if you yourself the trouble not even for your daily nourishment give will, then are you also not worth that you it eat.”
sentences.i: if you will not even take the trouble for your daily bread, then you are not worth the eating of it.”
sentences.n: die = ‘dir’; Möhe = ‘Mühe’; dine = ‘deine’; dägliche = ‘tägliche’; Narunge = ‘Nahrung’; wust = ‘willst’; werth is the 1857 spelling of ‘wert’; etest = ‘issest’, an old second-person subjunctive of ‘essen’.

sentences.t: Da word dat Männeken so bös un sehde he möst et doen:
sentences.l: Then became the manikin so angry and said he must it do:
sentences.i: At that the little man grew so angry, and said he must do it:
sentences.n: word = ‘wurde’; bös = ‘böse’; sehde = ‘sagte’; möst = ‘müsse/müßte’ — the subjunctive of reported speech once more.

sentences.t: he awerst nig fuhl, nam min lewe Männeken un drosch et duet dör (tüchtig durch).
sentences.l: he however not lazy, took my dear manikin and threshed him soundly through (soundly through).
sentences.i: but he, nothing loath, caught up my dear little man and gave him a thorough thrashing.
sentences.n: “nicht faul” is a set phrase — not slow about it, without more ado; fuhl = ‘faul’; nam = ‘nahm’. “min lewe Männeken”, my dear little man, is the teller stepping into his own tale for a moment, with dry sympathy for the creature about to be beaten. drosch = ‘drosch’, threshed, as grain is threshed; and “duet dör” carries the Grimms’ own gloss (tüchtig durch), soundly through.

sentences.t: Da schriege dat Männeken so viel
sentences.l: Then screamed the manikin so much
sentences.i: Then the little man screamed so
sentences.n: schriege = ‘schrie’; “so viel” again as the intensifier — ever so much.

sentences.t: un rep „hör up, hör up, un lat mie geweren, dann will ik die auck seggen wo de Künigsdöchter sied.“
sentences.l: and called, “stop, stop, and let me be, then will I you also tell where the king’s daughters are.”
sentences.i: and cried, “Stop, stop, and let me be, and I will tell you where the king’s daughters are.”
sentences.n: rep = ‘rief’; “hör up” = ‘hör auf’, stop; lat = ‘laß’; geweren = ‘gewähren’ — “einen gewähren lassen” is to let a person be, to leave off him; sied = ‘sind’, not ‘seit’.

sentences.t: Wie he dat hörde, häll hei up to slaen,
sentences.l: When he that heard, held he up to strike,
sentences.i: When he heard that, he left off striking,
sentences.n: hörde = ‘hörte’; “häll ... up” = ‘hielt auf’, left off; hei = ‘er’ — a second Low German word for ‘he’, standing alongside he; slaen = ‘schlagen’.

sentences.t: un dat Männeken vertelde he wör en Erdmänneken, un sulke wären mehr ase dusend,
sentences.l: and the manikin told he was an earth-manikin, and of such were more than a thousand,
sentences.i: and the little man told him he was an earth-man, and that there were more than a thousand of them,
sentences.n: vertelde = ‘erzählte’; wör = ‘wäre’; sulke = ‘solche’; dusend = ‘tausend’. The Erdmänneken of the title is one of the underground folk; the whole thousand of them come back at the end of the tale.

sentences.t: he mögte man mit ünne gaen, dann wulle he ünne wiesen wo de Künigsdöchter weren.
sentences.l: he might just with him go, then would he him show where the king’s daughters were.
sentences.i: he had only to come along with him, and he would show him where the king’s daughters were.
sentences.n: mögte = ‘möchte’; man here is Low German for ‘nur’, just, only — not the impersonal High German ‘man’, one, which it is spelled like; weren here = ‘wären’, from sein — not ‘werden’, to become; wulle = ‘wollte’; wiesen = ‘weisen/zeigen’, to show — again not the ‘Wiese’, meadow, that the spelling suggests.

sentences.t: Da wist he ünne en deipen Born, da is awerst kien Water inne west.
sentences.l: Then showed he him a deep well, there is however no water in it been.
sentences.i: Then he showed him a deep well, but there was no water in it.
sentences.n: wist = ‘wies’, showed — the past tense of the wiesen of the line before; Born is the old word for a well or spring, still living in the north; inne = ‘drin’.

sentences.t: Da segd dat Männeken he wuste wohl dat et sine Gesellen nig ehrlich mit ünne meinten,
sentences.l: Then says the manikin he knew well that his companions not honestly with him meant,
sentences.i: Then the little man said he knew well that his companions did not mean honestly by him,
sentences.n: wuste = ‘wußte’, knew — one letter from wist, ‘wies’, showed, in the line above, and a different verb altogether; et is an empty placeholder subject; Gesellen = fellows, companions. “es nicht ehrlich mit einem meinen” is to mean a person no good.

sentences.t: wenn he de Künigskinner erlösen wulle, dann möste he et alleine doen.
sentences.l: if he the king’s children deliver wanted, then must he it alone do.
sentences.i: if he wanted to deliver the king’s children, he would have to do it alone.
sentences.n: Künigskinner = ‘Königskinder’; erlösen, to deliver, to set free from a spell, is the standing word of these tales for undoing an enchantment; möste = ‘müßte’.

sentences.t: De beiden annern Broer wullen wohl auck geren de Künigsdöchter wier hewen,
sentences.l: The two other brothers wanted indeed also gladly the king’s daughters back to have,
sentences.i: The two other brothers would gladly have the king’s daughters back too,
sentences.n: Broer = ‘Brüder’; wullen = ‘wollten’; wohl = indeed, right enough; geren = ‘gern’; hewen = ‘haben’ again.

sentences.t: awerst se wullen der kiene Möge un Gefahr umme doen,
sentences.l: but they wanted for it no trouble and danger about do,
sentences.i: but they would go to no trouble and run no danger for it,
sentences.n: “der ... umme” = ‘darum’, split in two around the nouns — an old northern habit that German still keeps in ‘da ... für’. Möge = ‘Mühe’, the same word spelled Möhe earlier; “Mühe darum thun” is to take pains over a thing.

sentences.t: he möste so en grauten Korv nümmen, un möste sik mit sinen Hirschfänger un en Schelle darinne setten un sik herunter winnen laten:
sentences.l: he must such a great basket take, and must himself with his hunting-knife and a bell therein set and himself down let be wound:
sentences.i: he must take a great basket, and set himself in it with his hunting-knife and a bell, and have himself wound down:
sentences.n: grauten = ‘großen’; Korv = ‘Korb’; nümmen = ‘nehmen’; Schelle, a small bell, to ring as a signal; darinne = ‘darin’; “herunter winnen laten” = ‘herunterwinden lassen’ — the basket goes down the well on a rope and windlass. A Hirschfänger is a huntsman’s short sword, literally a deer-catcher.

sentences.t: unnen da wören drei Zimmer, in jeden sette ein Künigskind un hädde en Drachen mit villen Köppen to lusen,
sentences.l: down below there were three rooms, in each sat a king’s child and had a dragon with many heads to delouse,
sentences.i: down below there were three chambers, and in each sat a king’s daughter with a many-headed dragon to delouse,
sentences.n: unnen = ‘unten’; sette = ‘säße’ and hädde = ‘hätte’, both subjunctive — the little man is still reporting, not describing. villen = ‘vielen’; Köppen = ‘Köpfen’; lusen = ‘lausen’, to pick lice from. Combing the vermin out of a monster’s hair is menial work in these tales, and it is what the stolen daughters are set to.

sentences.t: den möste he de Köppe afschlagen.
sentences.l: to it must he the heads strike off.
sentences.i: and he must strike the heads off it.
sentences.n: den = ‘dem’, the dragon, in the dative — “einem den Kopf abschlagen”, to strike a creature’s head off; afschlagen = ‘abschlagen’.

sentences.t: Ase dat Erdmänneken nu dat alle sagd hadde, verschwand et.
sentences.l: When the earth-manikin now that all said had, vanished it.
sentences.i: When the earth-man had said all this, he vanished.
sentences.n: “dat alle” = ‘das alles’; et = ‘es’, for the neuter Männeken — grammar makes the creature an ‘it’ throughout, though the tale plainly means a person.

sentences.t: Ase’t Awend is, da kümmet de beiden annern un fraget wie et ün gaen hädde,
sentences.l: When it evening is, then come the two others and ask how it him gone had,
sentences.i: When evening came, the other two came and asked how it had gone with him,
sentences.n: “Ase’t” = ‘als es’, with the pronoun reduced to a hooked ’t; Awend = ‘Abend’, spelled Avend a page earlier; fraget = ‘fragen’; ün = ‘ihm’.

sentences.t: da segd he „o, so wit gud,“
sentences.l: then says he, “oh, so far good,”
sentences.i: and he said, “Oh, well enough so far,”
sentences.n: wit = ‘weit’; gud = ‘gut’.

sentences.t: un hädde keinen Minsken sehen, ase des Middags, da wer so ein klein Männeken kummen, de hädde ün umme en Stücksken Braud biddit,
sentences.l: and had no person seen, except at midday, then had such a little manikin come, he had him for a little piece of bread begged,
sentences.i: and had seen nobody, except that at midday a little man had come who had begged him for a little piece of bread,
sentences.n: His whole account runs on in the subjunctive of reported speech — hädde, wer, hädde — so that the ‘he said that’ need be said only once and the mood of the verb carries the rest. ase here = ‘als’ in the sense ‘except’; “des Middags” = ‘des Mittags’, a genitive of time; biddit = ‘gebeten’.

sentences.t: do he et ünne giewen hädde, hädde dat Männeken et fallen laten un hädde segd he mögtet ünne doch wier up nümmen,
sentences.l: when he it him given had, had the manikin it fall let and had said he might it him yet again up take,
sentences.i: and when he had given it to him, the little man had let it fall and had said would he pick it up for him again,
sentences.n: mögtet = ‘möchte es’, the verb with the pronoun et welded on to its end — the tale does this often (Ase’t, mögtet, willt).

sentences.t: wie he dat nig hädde doen wullt, da hädde et anfangen to puchen,
sentences.l: when he that not had do wanted, then had it begun to bluster,
sentences.i: and when he would not do it, it had begun to bluster,
sentences.n: wullt here = ‘gewollt’, the past participle, not the ‘willst’ it looks like; puchen = ‘pochen’ in its older sense, to bluster, to bully, to throw one’s weight about.

sentences.t: dat hädde he awerst unrecht verstan un hädde dat Männeken prügelt,
sentences.l: that had he however wrongly understood and had the manikin thrashed,
sentences.i: but he had taken that amiss and had thrashed the little man,
sentences.n: verstan = ‘verstanden’; prügelt = ‘geprügelt’. He is telling it slyly — the beating becomes a misunderstanding.

sentences.t: un da hädde et ünne vertellt wo de Künigsdöchter wären.
sentences.l: and then had it him told where the king’s daughters were.
sentences.i: and then it had told him where the king’s daughters were.
sentences.n: vertellt = ‘erzählt’; wären is subjunctive, still inside the report.

sentences.t: Da ärgerten sik de beiden so viel, dat se gehl un grön wören.
sentences.l: Then vexed themselves the two so much that they yellow and green were.
sentences.i: At that the two were so vexed that they turned yellow and green.
sentences.n: gehl = ‘gelb’; grön = ‘grün’. “Gelb und grün werden” is the German for turning livid with spite — the colours of envy rather than of sickness.

sentences.t: Den annern Morgen da gungen se to haupe an den Born un mackten Loose, wer sik dat erste in den Korv setten sulle,
sentences.l: The next morning then went they together to the well and made lots, who himself the first into the basket set should,
sentences.i: The next morning they went together to the well and drew lots for who should get into the basket first,
sentences.n: “to haupe” = ‘zuhauf/zusammen’, together; “mackten Loose” = ‘machten Loose’, cast lots; “dat erste” = ‘das erste [Mal]’, first.

sentences.t: da feel dat Loos wier den öllesten to, he mot sik darin setten un de Klingel mitnümmen.
sentences.l: then fell the lot again to the eldest, he must himself therein set and the bell take along.
sentences.i: and the lot fell to the eldest again; he had to get in and take the bell with him.
sentences.n: “feel ... to” = ‘fiel zu’, fell to; öllesten = ‘ältesten’, written here with two l and earlier with one; Klingel is the bell the plan called a Schelle; mitnümmen = ‘mitnehmen’.

sentences.t: Da segd he „wenn ik klingele, so mutt gi mik nur geschwinne wier herupwinnen.“
sentences.l: Then says he, “when I ring, then must you me just quickly again up-wind.”
sentences.i: Then he said, “When I ring, you must just wind me up again quickly.”
sentences.n: ik = ‘ich’; klingele = ‘klingle’; mutt = ‘müßt’; gi = ‘ihr’, you (plural) in the nominative — the ju further on is the same word in the object case; mik = ‘mich’; geschwinne = ‘geschwind’; herupwinnen = ‘heraufwinden’.

sentences.t: Ase he en bitken herunner is, da klingelte wat, da winnen se ünne wier heruper:
sentences.l: When he a little bit down is, then rang something, then wind they him again up:
sentences.i: When he was a little way down, something rang, and they wound him up again:
sentences.n: bitken = ‘bißchen’; herunner = ‘herunter’; wat = ‘was’, here in the sense ‘something’; winnen = ‘winden’; heruper = ‘herauf’. The tale leaves it open whether he rang out of fear or the bell knocked against the wall — it says only that something rang.

sentences.t: da sett sik de tweide herinne, de maket ewen sau:
sentences.l: then sets himself the second in there, he makes just so:
sentences.i: then the second got in, and he did just the same:
sentences.n: “sett sik” = ‘setzt sich’; herinne = ‘hinein’; ewen = ‘eben’, just; sau = ‘so’ in its Low German spelling — not the High German ‘Sau’, sow.

sentences.t: nu kümmet dann auck de Riege an den jungesten, de lät sik awerst gans drinne runner winnen.
sentences.l: now comes then also the turn to the youngest, he lets himself however quite all the way down wind.
sentences.i: now the turn came to the youngest, and he had himself wound right down to the bottom.
sentences.n: Riege = ‘Reihe’ — “die Reihe kommt an einen”, one’s turn comes; lät = ‘läßt’; “gans drinne” = ‘ganz drinnen’, all the way in; runner = ‘runter/herunter’.

sentences.t: Ase he ut den Korve stiegen is, da nümmet he sinen Hirschfänger un geit vor der ersten Doer staen un lustert,
sentences.l: When he out of the basket climbed is, then takes he his hunting-knife and goes before the first door stand and listens,
sentences.i: When he had climbed out of the basket, he took his hunting-knife, went and stood before the first door, and listened,
sentences.n: stiegen = ‘gestiegen’; Korve = ‘Korbe’, an old dative in ‑e; Doer = ‘Thür’, spelled Döre in the very next line; “geit ... staen” = ‘geht stehen’, goes and stands, a turn English has too; lustert = ‘lauscht/horcht’.

sentences.t: da hort he den Drachen gans lute schnarchen.
sentences.l: then hears he the dragon quite loudly snoring.
sentences.i: and he heard the dragon snoring very loudly.
sentences.n: hort = ‘hört’; lute = ‘laut’ with the old adverbial ‑e.

sentences.t: He macket langsam de Döre oppen,
sentences.l: He makes slowly the door open,
sentences.i: He slowly opened the door,
sentences.n: “die Thür aufmachen” is simply to open the door; oppen = ‘auf’, the separable particle standing at the end; Döre = ‘Thür’.

sentences.t: da sitt da de eine Künigsdochter un häd op eren Schot niegene (neun) Drachenköppe ligen un luset de.
sentences.l: there sits the one king’s daughter and has on her lap nine (nine) dragon-heads lying and louses them.
sentences.i: and there sat the one king’s daughter, with nine dragon heads lying in her lap, picking the lice out of them.
sentences.n: op = ‘auf’; eren = ‘ihren’; Schot = ‘Schoß’, lap; niegene carries the Grimms’ own gloss (neun); ligen = ‘liegen’; luset = ‘laust’; de at the end = ‘die’, them.

sentences.t: Da nümmet he sinen Hirschfänger un hogget to, da siet de niegne Koppe awe.
sentences.l: Then takes he his hunting-knife and hews to, then are the nine heads off.
sentences.i: Then he took his hunting-knife and struck, and the nine heads were off.
sentences.n: “hogget to” = ‘haut zu’, strikes home, the particle to marking the blow going in; siet = ‘sind’ — not ‘Seite’, side, which it is spelled like; niegne = ‘neun’, spelled a third way in as many lines; Koppe = ‘Köpfe’; awe = ‘ab’, off.

sentences.t: De Künigsdochter sprank up un fäl ünne um den Hals un drucket un piepete (küßte) ünn so viel,
sentences.l: The king’s daughter sprang up and fell him around the neck and pressed and kissed him ever so much,
sentences.i: The king’s daughter sprang up and fell on his neck and hugged and kissed him again and again,
sentences.n: sprank = ‘sprang’; fäl = ‘fiel’ — “einem um den Hals fallen”, to throw one’s arms round a person; drucket = ‘drückt’, hugs; piepete carries the Grimms’ own gloss (küßte); ünn = ‘ihn’.

sentences.t: un nümmet ihr Bruststücke, dat wor von rauen Golle west, un henget ünne dat umme.
sentences.l: and takes her breast-piece, that was of red gold been, and hangs it about him.
sentences.i: and took her breast-ornament, which was of red gold, and hung it about him.
sentences.n: Bruststücke = ‘Bruststück’, an ornament worn on the breast; wor = ‘war’; “rauen Golle” = ‘rothem Golde’ — red gold is the old epithet for gold of the purest kind; “henget ... umme” = ‘hängt um’.

sentences.t: Da geit he auck nach der tweiden Künigsdochter, de häd en Drachen mit sieven Köppe to lusen un erlöset de auck,
sentences.l: Then goes he also to the second king’s daughter, she has a dragon with seven heads to delouse, and delivers her too,
sentences.i: Then he went on to the second king’s daughter, who had a seven-headed dragon to delouse, and delivered her too,
sentences.n: häd = ‘hat’; sieven = ‘sieben’; erlöset = ‘erlöst’.

sentences.t: so de jungeste, de hadde en Drachen mit viere Köppen to lusen had, da geit he auck hinne.
sentences.l: so the youngest, she had a dragon with four heads to delouse had, then goes he also thither.
sentences.i: and so with the youngest, who had a four-headed dragon to delouse; to her he went as well.
sentences.n: viere = ‘vier’ with an old inflected ending; hinne = ‘hin’, thither. The sentence begins loosely with so, ‘and so likewise’, leaving its verb to be supplied from the clause before.

sentences.t: Do froget se sich alle so viel, un drucketen un piepeten ohne uphören.
sentences.l: Then rejoiced they all so much, and hugged and kissed without ceasing.
sentences.i: Then they all rejoiced so, and hugged and kissed without ceasing.
sentences.n: froget = ‘freuen sich’, rejoice — despite the spelling this is not the fraget, ‘fragen’, of other lines; drucketen and piepeten are the past plurals of the drucket and piepete just above; uphören = ‘aufhören’.

sentences.t: Da klingelte he sau harde, bis dat se owen hört.
sentences.l: Then rang he so hard, until that they above hear.
sentences.i: Then he rang so hard that they heard it up above.
sentences.n: sau = ‘so’; harde = ‘hart’; “bis dat” = ‘bis daß’; owen = ‘oben’, above — the same spelling that means ‘Ofen’, oven, at the end of the tale.

sentences.t: Da set he de Künigsdöchter ein nach der annern in den Korv un let se alle drei heruptrecken,
sentences.l: Then sets he the king’s daughters one after the other into the basket and lets them all three be drawn up,
sentences.i: Then he set the king’s daughters one after another into the basket and had all three drawn up,
sentences.n: set = ‘setzt’; let = ‘läßt’; heruptrecken = ‘heraufziehen’.

sentences.t: wie nu an ünne de Riege kümmt, da fallet ün de Woore (Worte) von den Erdmänneken wier bie, dat et sine Gesellen mit ünne nig gut meinden.
sentences.l: when now to him the turn comes, then fall to him the words (words) of the earth-manikin again in, that his companions with him not well meant.
sentences.i: and when his own turn came, the earth-man’s words came back to him, that his companions did not mean well by him.
sentences.n: “einem fällt etwas wieder bei” = ‘es fällt ihm wieder ein’, it comes back to him — a separable verb whose particle bie has drifted right to the end of the clause. Woore carries the Grimms’ own gloss (Worte); meinden = ‘meinten’.

sentences.t: Da nümmet he en groten Stein, de da ligt un legt ün in den Korv,
sentences.l: Then takes he a great stone that lies there and lays it into the basket,
sentences.i: So he took a great stone that was lying there and laid it in the basket,
sentences.n: groten = ‘großen’; ligt = ‘liegt’; ün here = ‘ihn’, the stone, and not the man.

sentences.t: ase de Korv da ungefähr bis in de Midde herup is, schnien de falsken Broer owen dat Strick af, dat de Korv mit den Stein up den Grund füll,
sentences.l: when the basket there roughly to the middle up is, cut the false brothers above the rope off, so that the basket with the stone to the bottom fell,
sentences.i: and when the basket was about halfway up, the false brothers cut the rope above, so that the basket and the stone fell to the bottom,
sentences.n: Midde = ‘Mitte’; herup = ‘herauf’; “schnien ... af” = ‘schnitten ab’; falsken = ‘falschen’, treacherous; Strick, the rope; füll = ‘fiel’.

sentences.t: un meinten he wöre nu daude,
sentences.l: and thought he were now dead,
sentences.i: and supposed he was dead now,
sentences.n: wöre = ‘wäre’, subjunctive, because it is what they took to be so and not what was; daude = ‘todt/tot’.

sentences.t: un laupet mit de drei Künigsdöchter wege un latet sik dervan verspreken dat se an ehren Vater seggen willt dat se beiden se erlöset hädden;
sentences.l: and run with the three king’s daughters away and let themselves promise thereto that they to their father say would that they two them delivered had;
sentences.i: and made off with the three king’s daughters, exacting a promise from them that they would tell their father that the two of them had delivered them;
sentences.n: laupet = ‘laufen’; wege = ‘weg’; “latet sik ... verspreken” = ‘lassen sich versprechen’, exact a promise; dervan = ‘davon/darauf’; ehren = ‘ihren’, their — not the verb ehren, to honour; willt = ‘wollen’, they will — not the ‘willst’ it is spelled like; “se beiden” = ‘sie beiden’, those two, the brothers.

sentences.t: da kümmet se tom Künig, un begert se tor Frugen.
sentences.l: then come they to the king and demand them to wife.
sentences.i: and so they came to the king and demanded them in marriage.
sentences.n: tom = ‘zum’; begert = ‘begehrt’; “tor Frugen” = ‘zur Frau’, in marriage — the reward proclaimed at the beginning of the tale.

sentences.t: Unnerdies geit de jungeste Jägerbursche gans bedröwet in den drei Kammern herummer un denket dat he nu wull sterwen möste,
sentences.l: Meanwhile goes the youngest huntsman quite grieved in the three chambers about and thinks that he now surely die must,
sentences.i: Meanwhile the youngest huntsman walked about the three chambers in deep grief, thinking he must surely die now,
sentences.n: Unnerdies = ‘unterdes’; herummer = ‘herum’; denket = ‘denkt’; wull here = ‘wohl’, surely, and not ‘wollte’; sterwen = ‘sterben’.

sentences.t: da süht he an der Wand ’n Fleutenpipe hangen,
sentences.l: then sees he on the wall a flute-pipe hanging,
sentences.i: when he saw a flute hanging on the wall,
sentences.n: süht = ‘sieht’; ’n = ‘eine’; Fleutenpipe = ‘Flötenpfeife’, a pipe or flute.

sentences.t: da segd he „worümme hengest du da wull, hier kann ja doch keiner lustig sin?“
sentences.l: then says he, “why do you hang there, I wonder — here surely nobody can merry be?”
sentences.i: and he said, “Why do you hang there? Nobody can be merry here.”
sentences.n: worümme = ‘warum’; hengest = ‘hängst’; wull = ‘wohl’, the particle that turns a question into a musing one; sin = ‘sein’, to be. He is speaking to the flute — a small thing, but it is that address which brings the rescue.

sentences.t: He bekucket auck de Drachenköppe, un segd „ju künnt mie nu auck nig helpen.“
sentences.l: He looks also at the dragon heads and says, “you can me now also not help.”
sentences.i: He looked at the dragon heads too, and said, “You cannot help me now either.”
sentences.n: bekucket = ‘beguckt’, looks over; ju = ‘ihr’, you (plural), here in the nominative where gi stood earlier; künnt = ‘könnt’; helpen = ‘helfen’.

sentences.t: He geit so mannigmal up un af spatzeren, dat de Erdboden davon glat werd.
sentences.l: He goes so many a time up and down walking, that the ground from it smooth becomes.
sentences.i: He walked up and down so many times that the floor grew smooth with it.
sentences.n: mannigmal = ‘manches Mal’; “up un af” = ‘auf und ab’; spatzeren = ‘spazieren’; Erdboden, the earthen floor; glat = ‘glatt’, worn smooth.

sentences.t: Up et lest, da kriegt he annere Gedanken,
sentences.l: At the last, then gets he other thoughts,
sentences.i: At last other thoughts came to him,
sentences.n: “andere Gedanken kriegen” is to think better of it, to take a different turn of mind.

sentences.t: da nümmet he de Fleutenpipen van der Wand un blest en Stücksken,
sentences.l: then takes he the flute from the wall and blows a little piece,
sentences.i: so he took the flute down from the wall and played a little tune,
sentences.n: blest = ‘bläst’; “en Stücksken” is the same diminutive that meant a piece of bread earlier — here a little piece of music, a tune.

sentences.t: up eenmahl kummet da so viele Erdmännekens, bie jeden Don, den he däht, kummt eint mehr:
sentences.l: all at once come there so many earth-manikins, at every note that he made comes one more:
sentences.i: all at once so many earth-men came, and at every note he sounded another one came:
sentences.n: “up eenmahl” = ‘auf einmal’; Don = ‘Ton’, a note; däht = ‘that/tat’ — “einen Ton thun” is to sound a note; eint = ‘eins’, one.

sentences.t: da blest he so lange dat Stücksken, bis det Zimmer stopte vull is.
sentences.l: then blows he so long the little piece until the room stuffed full is.
sentences.i: so he played the tune until the room was crammed full.
sentences.n: det = ‘das’; “stopte vull” = ‘stopfvoll’, packed full.

sentences.t: De fraget alle wat sin Begeren wöre,
sentences.l: They ask all what his desire were,
sentences.i: They all asked what his wish was,
sentences.n: De = ‘die’, they; fraget = ‘fragen’ — the true ‘fragen’ this time, unlike the froget above; Begeren = ‘Begehren’, desire, request; wöre is subjunctive because the question is a reported one.

sentences.t: da segd he he wull geren wier up de Ere an Dages Licht,
sentences.l: then says he he would gladly again up on the earth into day’s light,
sentences.i: and he said he would gladly be up on the earth again in the light of day,
sentences.n: wull = ‘wollte’; Ere = ‘Erde’, spelled Eere in the opening block; “an Dages Licht” = ‘an das Tageslicht’. The verb of motion is simply left out after the modal, as German leaves it out — he would gladly [go] up.

sentences.t: da fatten sie ünne alle an, an jeden Spir (Faden) Haar, wat he up sinen Koppe hadde,
sentences.l: then take they him all hold of, by every thread (thread) of hair that he on his head had,
sentences.i: so they all took hold of him, by every single hair he had on his head,
sentences.n: “fatten ... an” = ‘fassen an’, take hold of; Spir carries the Grimms’ own gloss (Faden) — a thread, a single filament; sinen = ‘seinem’.

sentences.t: un sau fleiget se mit ünne herupper his up de Ere.
sentences.l: and so fly they with him up as far as onto the earth.
sentences.i: and so they flew up with him right out onto the earth.
sentences.n: fleiget = ‘fliegen’; herupper = ‘herauf/hinauf’; his = ‘bis’, as far as.

sentences.t: Wie he owen is, geit he glick nach den Künigsschlott, wo grade de Hochtit mit der einen Künigsdochter sin sulle,
sentences.l: When he above is, goes he straight to the king’s castle, where just then the wedding with the one king’s daughter to be was,
sentences.i: When he was up, he went straight to the king’s castle, where the wedding with the one king’s daughter was just about to be held,
sentences.n: owen = ‘oben’; glick = ‘gleich’, straight away; Künigsschlott = ‘Königsschloß’; grade = ‘gerade’; Hochtit = ‘Hochzeit’; “sin sulle” = ‘sein sollte’, was to take place.

sentences.t: un geit up den Zimmer, wo de Künig mit sinen drei Döchtern is.
sentences.l: and goes into the room where the king with his three daughters is.
sentences.i: and went into the room where the king was with his three daughters.
sentences.n: “up den Zimmer” = ‘auf das Zimmer’, into the chamber; Döchtern = ‘Töchtern’.

sentences.t: Wie ünne da de Kinner seihet, da wered se gans beschwämt (ohnmächtig).
sentences.l: When him there the children see, then become they quite faint (unconscious).
sentences.i: When the children saw him there, they fell into a dead faint.
sentences.n: ünne stands first as the object — Low German, like German, can put the object in the front slot and the verb second; seihet = ‘sehen’; wered = ‘werden’; beschwämt carries the Grimms’ own gloss (ohnmächtig), swooning away.

sentences.t: Da werd de Künig so böse un let ünne glick in een Gefängnisse setten,
sentences.l: Then becomes the king so angry and has him straight away into a prison put,
sentences.i: At that the king grew so angry that he had him put straight into prison,
sentences.n: “let ... setten” = ‘läßt setzen’, has him put — German uses ‘lassen’ where English says ‘have someone do’; een = ‘ein’; Gefängnisse = ‘Gefängniß’ with an old dative ‑e.

sentences.t: weil he meint he hädde den Kinnern en Leid anne daen.
sentences.l: because he thinks he had to the children a harm done.
sentences.i: because he thought he had done the children some harm.
sentences.n: “einem ein Leid anthun” is to do a person harm; “anne daen” = ‘angethan’, with the particle standing free; Kinnern = ‘Kindern’; hädde is subjunctive because it is what the king supposed.

sentences.t: Ase awer de Künigsdöchter wier to sik kummt, da biddet se so viel he mogte ünne doch wier lose laten.
sentences.l: But when the king’s daughters to themselves again come, then beg they ever so much he might him yet again loose let.
sentences.i: But when the king’s daughters came to themselves again, they begged and begged that he would let him go.
sentences.n: “to sik kummt” = ‘zu sich kommt’, come round; biddet = ‘bitten’; mogte = ‘möchte’; “lose laten” = ‘loslassen’, let go.

sentences.t: De Künig fraget se worümme, da segd se dat se dat nig vertellen dorften,
sentences.l: The king asks them why, then say they that they that not tell might,
sentences.i: The king asked them why, and they said they were not allowed to tell,
sentences.n: dorften = ‘durften’ — the promise the brothers exacted still binds them; vertellen = ‘erzählen’.

sentences.t: awerst de Vaer de segd se sullen et en Owen (Ofen) vertellen.
sentences.l: but the father, he says they should it to an oven (oven) tell.
sentences.i: but the father said they should tell it to an oven.
sentences.n: Vaer = ‘Vater’; sullen = ‘sollten’; Owen carries the Grimms’ own gloss (Ofen) — and it is the same spelling that meant ‘oben’, above, a few lines back. Telling a secret to the stove is a standing device in these tales: an oath not to tell binds the speaker only against telling a person.

sentences.t: Da geit he herut un lustert an de Döre un hört alles.
sentences.l: Then goes he out and listens at the door and hears everything.
sentences.i: Then he went out and listened at the door and heard it all.
sentences.n: herut = ‘heraus’. It is the king who slips out: he tells them to speak to the oven and then stands and eavesdrops.

sentences.t: Da lät he de beiden an en Galgen hängen, un den einen givt he de jungeste Dochter:
sentences.l: Then has he the two on a gallows hanged, and to the one gives he the youngest daughter:
sentences.i: So he had the two of them hanged on a gallows, and to the one he gave the youngest daughter:
sentences.n: “lät ... hängen” = ‘läßt hängen’, has hanged; givt = ‘gibt’. “den einen” is the young huntsman — having been ‘the youngest’ all through the tale, he is set off here simply as ‘the one’.

sentences.t: un da trok ik en Paar gläserne Schohe an, un da stott ik an en Stein, da segd et „klink!“
sentences.l: and then drew I a pair of glass shoes on, and then struck I against a stone, then said it, “clink!”
sentences.i: and then I put on a pair of glass shoes, and I struck against a stone, and it said, “Clink!”
sentences.n: The teller steps into his own tale in the last line — ik, ‘I’ — with a stock closing formula: he claims to have been at the wedding and to have come away with nothing to show. “trok ... an” = ‘zog an’, put on; stott = ‘stieß’.

sentences.t: da wören se caput.
sentences.l: then were they broken.
sentences.i: and they were done for.
sentences.n: caput = ‘kaputt’, broken to bits. The glass shoes shatter, and with them the teller’s claim to have been there at all — the tale ends on a shrug.

glossary.a: a — ah! (exclamation, = High German ‘ach/ah’; not the letter A)
glossary.acht: acht — eight (numeral; “en acht Dage” = an die acht Tage; not die Acht, heed)
glossary.beeten: beißen — bit (3rd pl. past; Low German = bissen, not the Low German beeten, a little bit)
glossary.bös: böse — angry (short form; here angry rather than wicked)
glossary.die: dir — to you (Low German dative pronoun = High German ‘dir’; in this tale never the article ‘die’)
glossary.do: da, dann — then, there (Low German); but in “do Diske” = zu, to (zu Tische, to table)
glossary.doet: thun — do (3rd pl.; Low German = thun/tun, “dat doet se” = das thun sie)
glossary.ehren: ihr — their (possessive, acc. sg. masc.; Low German = ihren; not the verb ehren, to honour)
glossary.gans: ganz — quite, entirely (Low German; not die Gans, goose)
glossary.hei: er — he (Low German, a second word for ‘he’ beside he; not the interjection ‘hei’, hey)
glossary.hewen: haben — to have (Low German infinitive; not the Low German hewen, Himmel/heaven)
glossary.hätt: haben — has (3rd sg.; Low German = hat, not hätte)
glossary.hört: hören — hears; also 3rd pl. in ‑t (Low German = hört/hören)
glossary.inne: drinnen, darin — inside, in it (Low German)
glossary.ju: ihr — you (pl.; here the nominative, beside gi)
glossary.koppe: der Kopf — heads (Low German pl. = Köpfe; also dat. sg., “up sinen Koppe”)
glossary.lett: lassen — lets (3rd sg.; Low German = läßt, “lett ... fallen” = läßt fallen, drops; not the Low German lett, looks/seems)
glossary.lewen: lieb — dear (inflected; Low German = lieben, “mine lewen Süsterkes” = meine lieben Schwesterchen; not ‘leben’, to live)
glossary.mal: mal — once; just (adverb and coaxing particle, = High German ‘einmal’/‘mal’; not the noun das Mal)
glossary.man: nur — just, only (Low German; not the impersonal High German ‘man’, one)
glossary.n: ’n — ein, eine, einen (the reduced article; here not the pronoun ‘ihn’)
glossary.nah: nach — to, toward (Low German; not ‘nah’, near)
glossary.paar: das Paar — pair (“en Paar Schohe” = ein Paar Schuhe, a pair of shoes; not ein paar, a few)
glossary.satt: sitzen — sat (3rd sg. past; Low German = saß, “de Baum de satt so vull” = der Baum saß so voll; not the adjective ‘satt’, sated)
glossary.sau: so — so, thus (Low German; not die Sau, sow)
glossary.schlechte: schlecht — badly (adverb with the old ‑e; “et geit mie gans schlechte” = es geht mir ganz schlecht — the plain sense, not the older ‘poor, mean’)
glossary.sett: setzen — sets (3rd sg.; Low German = setzt, “sett sik” = setzt sich)
glossary.sied: sein — are (3rd pl.; Low German = sind, not ‘seit’, since)
glossary.siet: sein — are (3rd pl.; Low German = sind, not die Seite, side)
glossary.sin: sein — his; and also: to be (Low German; both senses occur in this tale)
glossary.stiegen: steigen — climbed (past participle; Low German = gestiegen, in “is ... stiegen”)
glossary.stücke: das Stück — piece (singular with the old ‑e; Low German “en Stücke” = ein Stück)
glossary.unrecht: unrecht — wrongly, amiss (adverb; “unrecht verstan” = unrecht verstanden, taken amiss; not the noun das Unrecht)
glossary.wartet: warten — wait (3rd pl. present; Low German makes the plural in ‑et, so = warten)
glossary.was: sein — was, i.e. High German ‘war’ (3rd sg. past; not the High German ‘was’, what)
glossary.wat: was — what; also ‘etwas’, something (“da klingelte wat”), and the relative ‘was/which’ (Low German)
glossary.wege: weg — away (Low German with an old ‑e; not die Wege, ways)
glossary.wer: wer, sein — who, whoever; and in “da wer ... kummen” = wäre (past subjunctive of sein), had come
glossary.weren: sein — were (past subjunctive pl.; Low German = wären; not ‘werden’, to become)
glossary.wiese: die Weise — way, manner (‘ut der Wiese’ = aus der Weise, out of the ordinary — the Grimms gloss it über alle Maßen; not die Wiese, meadow)
glossary.wiesen: weisen, zeigen — to show (Low German infinitive; not die Wiese, meadow)
glossary.willt: wollen — want, will (3rd pl.; Low German = wollen, not ‘willst’)
glossary.worden: werden — became (3rd pl. past; = wurden, not the passive participle geworden)
glossary.wull: wohl, wollen — surely, I wonder (particle, = High German ‘wohl’); and also ‘wollte’, wanted — both senses occur in this tale
glossary.wullt: wollen — wanted (past participle; Low German = gewollt, not ‘willst’)
